doc.title: Bill Kirchner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2021

title: Cannonball Adderley
summary: Kirchner praises Adderley as a great player and communicator and hears Coltrane's influence on his playing, e.g. 'Fun' on Mercy Mercy Mercy.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: Okay. Let me run a couple of names by you, see if you have anything to opine about. Cannonball Adderley.

Oh one of my favorite players. Wonderful player you know. I heard him, I heard his band with Nat live at a festival in Cleveland in the late 60s, you know the band with Joe Zawinul and Victor Gaskin and Roy McCurdy. I mean part of the fun of Cannonball, I mean he was so good with audiences. I mean when you listen to live Cannonball records they usually kept his audience raps on there and you could hear how good he was — he was a former school teacher so he really connected with audiences on a, not just a musical level but on a very personal level as well. And he was such a great player. I mean I think it’s only been in the past couple of decades that people have really been giving him his due for how good he really was. He was a staggeringly good player.
He surely was, and I have — just last week I was playing some of his last recordings, and he could go fairly out himself when he wanted to.

Well he spent two years standing next to Coltrane with Miles. I mean when you listen to hit records of his that he made after he played with Coltrane for a couple of years there’s a, you know there’s a real Coltrane influence in his playing. Like you know the album called “Mercy Mercy Mercy?”
There’s a tune on there called “Fun.”
Yeah. Right after “Games,” just before “Games,” right?

Yeah, but on “Fun” I mean there’s a real Coltrane influence on some of the lines that he plays and some of the harmonies that he uses. He learned a lot from Coltrane. He was a very smart guy so it was impossible for him not to pick up a lot when he was with Miles and Coltrane.
